title: e2e-latency-profiling-traces-iter1
content:
Goal:
Capture and analyze end-to-end latency traces for the serving runtime across typical workloads to identify p50/p95/p99 bottlenecks and actionable mitigations. This doc contains raw trace summaries, per-stage breakdowns, anomalies we observed, hypotheses, and immediate recommendations.

Background / test setup (short):
- Environment: staging-serving-cluster (dedicated pool, 4x A40 per node), runtime: v1.14.2 branch: perf/continuous-batching
- Models: rw-7b (baseline small), rw-70b (baseline large), rw-70b-quant (int8 variant)
- Clients: 50 concurrent virtual clients, Poisson arrival with mean QPS 20 for steady tests; burst tests with 200 concurrent clients
- Typical request sizes used: short (prompt 32 tokens, max_tokens 64), medium (prompt 256, max_tokens 256), long (prompt 1024, max_tokens 1024)
- Recording: full trace (client send -> network -> edge-router -> ingress proxy -> runtime queue -> runtime compute (token loop) -> kv-cache lookup -> serialization -> response) with millisecond granularity. Annotations for cache hit/miss and batch size per request.

High-level summary:
- p50 is generally dominated by compute time for medium/long requests (expected). p95/p99 tails are dominated by queueing + stragglers in compute stage and occasional serialization/GC pauses on the runtime host.
- Small requests (short prompts) show excellent p50 (~45ms) but long p99 tail (~350-600ms) due to batching delays and network jitter in bursts.
- Long requests show large absolute p95/p99 dominated by token generation; however relative overhead from routing and serialization increases with sequence length.

Representative aggregated numbers (median of test windows, values in ms):
- rw-7b, short requests (batching enabled): p50=45, p95=120, p99=380
- rw-7b, medium: p50=180, p95=420, p99=980
- rw-7b, long: p50=820, p95=1450, p99=2700
- rw-70b, short: p50=120, p95=420, p99=1250
- rw-70b, medium: p50=720, p95=1500, p99=3100
- rw-70b-quant, medium: p50=420, p95=950, p99=2100

Per-stage breakdown (typical p95 window; percentages add to ~100, times ms):
- Example: rw-7b medium p95=420ms
  - Client -> edge network: 18ms (4%)
  - Edge router / auth check: 12ms (3%)
  - Ingress proxy / TLS handshake (reused conn): 8ms (2%)
  - Runtime queue / batching wait: 120ms (29%)  <-- large contributor to tail
  - Compute (token loop) incl. KV cache lookups: 220ms (52%)
  - Serialization / HTTP encode: 30ms (7%)
  - Post-processing (safety, format): 12ms (3%)

- Example: rw-70b medium p99=3100ms
  - Network: 35ms (1%)
  - Router & ingress: 35ms (1%)
  - Queue / batching: 450ms (14%)
  - Compute (GPU kernels + kernel queueing + cross-GPU sync): 2350ms (76%)
  - Serialization + GC on host: 230ms (7%)

Observed patterns and anomalies:
1) Queueing-induced p99: We see many p99 tails where queue wait time is the biggest spike (short requests especially). Cause: batching policy with high max_batch_delay (default 50ms) + bursty arrivals. Small requests wait to fill batch.
2) Compute stragglers on 70B: p99 dominated by a few requests blocked on cross-GPU synchronization (allreduce / kernel enqueue ordering). Trace correlates with GPU_util variance and infrequent kernel-launch stalls.
3) Serialization / runtime-host GC spikes: multiple p99 events show a ~150-300ms serialization pause on the runtime host, often matching Python GC or large JSON encoding for long responses. Run-time flamegraphs show spikes in json.dumps and list comprehension in response builder.
4) KV-cache effect: cache hits reduce compute by ~30–40% on average for medium requests, but hit-rate variance causes tail amplification for sessions with many misses. Traces show cache-miss requests often get additional 40–120ms due to cache population logic (synchronous).
5) Network jitter: rare (~2% of p99) where upstream network retransmits add ~100–300ms. Mostly in burst tests across regions.

Detailed trace examples (short, medium):
- Short (rw-7b, p99 sample): total=560ms -> queue=300ms, compute=200ms, serialization=40ms. Annotations: batch_size=16 (under a burst), cache_hit=true, arrival_time cluster (many concurrent). Notes: large queue wait due to waiting for batch to fill (we observed batch_fill timing showing slow producers spending 50ms).
- Medium (rw-70b, p99 sample): total=3250ms -> queue=420ms, compute=2500ms, serialization=330ms. GPU telemetry: GPU0 queue stalled for 400ms waiting on kernel completion on GPU1 (cross-device sync).

Hypotheses (root causes):
- Default batching policy is too aggressive for short prompt patterns; high max_batch_delay reduces p50 for singletons but increases p99 under burst.
- Cross-GPU kernel ordering / sync issue for large models occasionally creates long kernel stalls leading to compute stragglers. Possibly caused by recent kernel selector change in commit abc123 (see linked PR).
- Synchronous KV cache population and response serialization in Python event loop leads to GC-induced tail events on long responses.
- Multi-tenant packing on some nodes introduces noisy neighbor effects (CPU contention affecting serialization/GC and the runtime event loop).

Immediate recommendations (low-to-medium effort):
- Adjust batching policy per model/route: lower max_batch_delay for routes that predominantly serve short prompts (experiment: max_batch_delay=8ms for short routes).
- Enable adaptive batching: enforce max latency SLO per request to prevent excessive waiting during bursts.
- Make KV cache population async: introduce a background population path so request critical path doesn't block on disk/serialization writes. (Ticket JIRA-SRV-1124)
- Move serialization of responses to C++ path or use ujson/cython for large payloads to reduce Python GC impact. Quick win: replace json.dumps with orjson for large responses (benchmarked ~3x faster).
- Add kernel launch ordering guard or fallback on kernel selector for rw-70b when sequences >512 to avoid pathological kernel combos.

Longer-term / higher-effort items:
- Rework cross-GPU sync patterns to reduce blocking on single slow GPU; investigate pipelined attention kernels and kernel fusion (research spike allocated).
- Introduce per-node CPU isolation / cpuset config to prevent noisy neighbors from affecting runtime process.
- Improve batching algorithm to mix request size and SLO awareness (content-aware batching).
- Add end-to-end synthetic trace harness that can reproduce bursts deterministically (to aid perf regressions).

Next steps / action items (owners):
- Evelyn: open perf regression PR to switch json.dumps -> orjson for response encoding (PR drafted, see linked PR). Target: staging rollout by 2026-03-10.
- Miguel: run controlled experiments with max_batch_delay=8/16/32ms for short-route traffic and produce new traces (JIRA: JIRA-SRV-1127). Due: 2026-03-09.
- Asha: investigate GPU kernel selector changes from commit abc123 and reproduce cross-GPU stall locally; propose patch or rollback. (Investigate w/ perf tools). Due: 2026-03-12.
- Jordan: prototype async KV population path and measure p99 improvements on medium workloads. (JIRA-SRV-1124). Due: 2026-03-15.

Open questions / things to validate:
- Are the p99 compute stragglers correlated with specific GPU driver versions? (need GPU driver + CUDA trace collection).
- Does orjson introduce any regression in memory usage or edge-case encoding differences for our telemetry formats? Run integration tests.
- Should we offer per-tenant batching profiles to let high-SLA tenants opt out of aggressive batching?

Notes / miscellaneous:
- Raw traces are saved under: /mnt/staging-traces/serving-runtime/2026-02-20/* (big tar files, see Confluence page CONFLUENCE-6789 for retrieval instructions).
- Short-term benchmark: switching to orjson + async cache population simulated on staging yields a p99 reduction for medium rw-7b from ~980ms -> ~640ms in our initial microtests (non-production slice).
- Follow-up: need to run end-to-end A/B tests with traffic mix matching production (90% short, 8% medium, 2% long) to pick optimal batching config.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing a p99 short-request tail locally:
- Use burst client harness (bench/clients/burst_sim.py) with 200 concurrent clients, Poisson arrival 20ms mean, route: short_prompt_route, batching config: default (max_batch_delay=50ms).
- Collect runtime logs with TRACE level and GPU metrics with nvidia-smi --query and nvprof sampling for the time window.
- Filter traces for requests with batch_size>=12 and inspect queue wait time.

Tagging/References: JIRA-SRV-1124 (KV cache), JIRA-SRV-1127 (batching experiments), CONFLUENCE-6789 (raw traces + retrieval), PR#436 (orjson change).
